The woylie (Bettongia penicillata) has a life history unfolding across a remarkably compressed developmental timeline under the thermoregulatory conditions typical of basal mammalian metabolism, estimated at 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C]. Gestation in this small potoroid marsupial is exceptionally brief, lasting only 18 days [tg = 18 days], a duration that aligns with the general pattern among macropodoids where a short uterine gestation is followed by an extended period of pouch development at a temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C]. Field studies conducted in the Upper Warren region of Western Australia indicate that female woylies give birth to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], with females capable of producing approximately 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters per year]. This combined reproductive output, though modest, is offset by continuous breeding opportunities across favorable seasons. The neonatal woylie emerges from the birth canal weighing a mere 0.29 grams [Wwb = 0.29 grams], a minuscule body mass that is typical of marsupial neonates and reflects the energetic economy of the extremely abbreviated gestation period at 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C]. This altricial newborn immediately crawls to the pouch, where it will undergo the majority of its morphological development.

The pouch young of the woylie experiences a prolonged period of dependency, with weaning occurring at approximately 150 days since birth [tx = approximately 150 days since birth] under the same thermal regime of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C] that characterizes endothermic maintenance. By this developmental milestone, the juvenile has achieved a wet weight at weaning of 500 grams [Wwx = 500 grams], representing a nearly 1,700-fold increase over its birth mass, a growth trajectory that is energetically demanding but typical for potoroids exploiting high-quality fungal diets. The transition to nutritional independence marks a critical ecological phase; during this period, the weaned juvenile begins to forage independently for the underground sporocarps of ectomycorrhizal fungi that constitute the bulk of its diet, while still maintaining some association with the maternal home range. This weaning mass of 500 grams [Wwx = 500 grams] represents approximately one-third of the adult body size, a point at which the skeletal and digestive systems are sufficiently developed to process solid food efficiently. Comparative data from other bettong species suggest that this weaning mass allows for a relatively rapid completion of somatic growth before the onset of reproductive maturation.

Sexual maturity in the woylie is attained at 180 days since birth [tp = 180 days since birth], a milestone that occurs shortly after the juvenile has become nutritionally independent and has completed the majority of its early somatic growth at a temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C]. Measured at the same basal temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C], this age at puberty is relatively early compared to many other Australian macropods of similar adult body size, reflecting the woylie's semelparous-adjacent life history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction over extended growth. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum body mass attained by fully grown adults, has been recorded at 1500 grams [Wwi = 1500 grams], a value that places Bettongia penicillata among the smaller potoroids and distinguishes it from its larger relatives such as Bettongia tropica. This adult mass of 1500 grams [Wwi = 1500 grams] is generally achieved by the time the individual reaches approximately one year of age, following which growth slows considerably as resources are diverted toward reproduction. The rapid attainment of both puberty and adult body mass within the first year of life is a hallmark of the woylie's r-selected life history strategy, which allows populations to recover quickly following environmental perturbations or population declines.

Woylie females exhibit continuous reproductive physiology, capable of breeding throughout much of the year when conditions are favorable, though maximum reproductive rates have been documented at 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C]. Under these optimal thermal conditions for gestation, the maintenance and development of the embryo proceed at a consistent metabolic pace. The 3 litters per year [F_R_i = 3 litters per year], each consisting of a single pup [N_R_i = each consisting of a single pup], result in a maximum annual reproductive output of three offspring per adult female, a figure that is relatively modest compared to many dasyurid marsupials but typical for potoroids. This maximum reproduction rate is constrained by the species' specialized dietary requirements and the energetic demands of lactating a single pouch young through its extended development. Resource availability, particularly the seasonal fruiting of hypogeous fungi, likely mediates whether females achieve the full potential of three litters per year or are forced to skip or delay breeding events. Comparisons with the brush-tailed bettong (Bettongia lesueur) suggest that the woylie's higher frequency of reproduction is offset by its smaller average litter size, resulting in a similar lifetime reproductive output.

Maximum lifespan in the woylie has been recorded at 18.8 years [am = 18.8 years] under captive conditions, a remarkably long duration for a mammal of this body size that reflects the protective benefits of a marsupial life history and low extrinsic mortality in managed environments at a temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C]. Field-based estimates, however, suggest a considerably shorter lifespan in the wild, likely on the order of 4 to 6 years, due to predation by introduced foxes and feral cats, habitat fragmentation, and disease. This longevity of 18.8 years [am = 18.8 years] was recorded in individuals maintained at a stable body temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C], underscoring the energetic efficiency of the woylie's low basal metabolic rate and its ability to delay reproductive senescence over an extended period. The extreme difference between captive and wild longevity highlights the severity of threats facing wild populations, which have declined dramatically across much of the species' historical range in southwestern Australia. Conservation programs focusing on predator-free fenced reserves and island translocations have successfully leveraged the species' capacity for extended reproductive life, allowing females to produce pups well into their second decade of life, thereby enhancing population recovery rates despite the small litter sizes.
